title: Inequalities of Combined Functions
overview: How many houses should a developer build? Which order sizes keep shipping costs down? When will a town outgrow its services? Questions like these have a **range** of answers, found by solving inequalities of combined functions. You will compare functions graphically and algebraically, use difference and quotient functions, and solve inequalities with technology when algebra cannot.
objectives: Determine where $f(x) > g(x)$ by finding intersections and testing intervals.
Illustrate inequalities visually, with a difference function, and with a quotient function – and know the limits of each.
Solve inequalities graphically when algebraic methods are not available.
Solve profit, inventory and planning problems involving inequalities.
Express solutions in interval notation and interpret them in context.

lessons.title: Comparing Two Functions
lessons.body:
Business and science questions often ask **when** one quantity is bigger than another: when is revenue more than cost? when does the population exceed the services available? These are **inequalities of combined functions**.

> $f(x) > g(x)$ for the $x$-values where the graph of $f$ lies **above** the graph of $g$.

**Strategy**
1. Find the points of intersection, where $f(x) = g(x)$ (algebraically if possible, otherwise with technology).
2. The intersections split the x-axis into intervals.
3. On each interval, one function stays above the other – test one point.

### Example
$f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = (x - 2)^2$.

Intersections: $x = (x - 2)^2 \Rightarrow x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0 \Rightarrow (x - 1)(x - 4) = 0$, so $x = 1$ or $x = 4$: points $(1, 1)$ and $(4, 4)$.

* $f(x) > g(x)$ on $(1, 4)$ (test $x = 2$: $2 > 0$ ✓)
* $g(x) > f(x)$ on $(-\infty, 1) \cup (4, \infty)$

```plot
title: f(x) = x is above g(x) = (x − 2)² on (1, 4)
f: x | label=f(x) = x
f: (x-2)^2 | label=g(x) = (x − 2)²
domain: -1, 6
range: -1, 8
points: (1,1), (4,4)
```

Interval notation reminder: $(1, 4)$ means $1 < x < 4$; square brackets include endpoints.

lessons.title: Three Ways to Illustrate an Inequality
lessons.body:
**Method 1 – Compare the graphs visually.** Graph both functions in different colours and see where one is above the other.

**Method 2 – The difference function.**
$$f(x) > g(x) \iff f(x) - g(x) > 0$$
Graph $y = f(x) - g(x)$ (by superposition or algebra) and find where it is **above the x-axis**. For the example: $f(x) - g(x) = x - (x - 2)^2 = -x^2 + 5x - 4$, positive on $(1, 4)$.

```plot
title: Difference function y = −x² + 5x − 4 is positive on (1, 4)
f: -x^2 + 5*x - 4
domain: -1, 6
range: -6, 4
points: (1,0), (4,0)
```

**Method 3 – The quotient function.** If $g(x) > 0$:
$$f(x) > g(x) \iff \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} > 1$$
Graph $y = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ with the line $y = 1$.

**Cautions for Method 3**
* It only works where $g(x) > 0$. If $g(x) < 0$, dividing by it **reverses** the inequality.
* It is undefined where $g(x) = 0$; check such points separately. In the example, $g(2) = 0$ and $f(2) = 2$, so $f(2) > g(2)$ even though the quotient does not exist there.

| Method | Advantage | Disadvantage |
|---|---|---|
| Visual | quick, intuitive | hard to read exact intersections |
| Difference | one graph vs the x-axis; algebra-friendly | requires simplifying |
| Quotient | shows ratios ("how many times bigger") | sign and zero issues with $g$ |

lessons.title: Inequalities That Need Technology
lessons.body:
Some inequalities cannot be solved with algebra, for example $\sin x > \log x$ (a trig function and a logarithmic function). Solve them **graphically**:

1. Graph $y = \sin x$ and $y = \log x$ (radian mode).
2. Find the intersections with technology: $x \approx 2.70$, $7.33$ and $8.26$.
3. $\log x$ exists only for $x > 0$ (asymptote at $x = 0$).
4. $\sin x$ is above $\log x$ on $(0, 2.70) \cup (7.33, 8.26)$.

```plot
title: sin x > log x on (0, 2.70) ∪ (7.33, 8.26)
f: sin(x) | label=sin x
f: log(x) | label=log x
domain: 0.05, 12
range: -1.5, 1.5
points: (2.696,0.431), (7.328,0.865), (8.264,0.917)
```

**Why are there no solutions for $x > 10$?** For $x > 10$, $\log x > 1 \ge \sin x$, so the log curve is always above.

On a graphing calculator, entering an inequality such as $Y_1 > Y_2$ (TEST menu) in Dot mode plots 1 where it is true and 0 where it is false – a quick visual check.

lessons.title: Business Applications: When Is It Profitable?
lessons.body:
For a business, **profit occurs where revenue > cost**, i.e. where $P = R - C > 0$. The intersections of $R$ and $C$ are the **break-even points**, and maximum profit occurs where $R$ exceeds $C$ by the greatest amount – the maximum of $P = R - C$.

### Housing developer
Fixed cost \$8 million, variable cost \$65 000 per house: $C(n) = 8 + 0.065n$ (millions). Revenue $R(n) = 1.6\sqrt{n}$ (millions).

* Solve $1.6\sqrt{n} = 8 + 0.065n$. Let $u = \sqrt n$: $0.065u^2 - 1.6u + 8 = 0$, so $u \approx 6.98$ or $17.64$, giving $n \approx 49$ and $n \approx 311$.
* The developer makes a profit building between about **49 and 311** houses.
* $P = 1.6u - 8 - 0.065u^2$ is largest at $u = \dfrac{1.6}{0.13} \approx 12.3$, i.e. $n \approx 151$ houses, with $P \approx \text{\textdollar}1.85$ million.

```plot
title: Profit region: R(n) = 1.6√n above C(n) = 8 + 0.065n
f: 1.6*sqrt(x) | label=R(n)
f: 8 + 0.065*x | label=C(n)
domain: 0, 420
range: 0, 40
points: (48.7,11.17), (311.3,28.23)
ticks: 50, 5
```

### Inventory control
Cost of shipping and storing $n$ computers: $C(n) = 1.5n + \dfrac{200\,000}{n}$ – a linear part plus a rational part.

To keep $C(n) < 1500$: multiply by $n > 0$ → $1.5n^2 - 1500n + 200\,000 < 0$. The quadratic formula gives $n \approx 158$ and $842$, so orders of **159 to 841** keep costs down (limited to 750 by warehouse size). The minimum cost occurs at about $n = 365$, where $C \approx \text{\textdollar}1095$.

keyTerms.definition: A statement such as $f(x) > g(x)$; its solution is the set of $x$-values where the graph of $f$ is above the graph of $g$.
$y = f(x) - g(x)$; $f > g$ exactly where it is positive (above the x-axis).
Intersections of revenue and cost curves; between them (if $R$ is above) the business is profitable.
$(a, b)$ means $a < x < b$; $[a, b]$ includes the endpoints; $\cup$ joins intervals.

formulas.name: Difference method
formulas.meaning: Graph the difference and look above the x-axis.

formulas.name: Quotient method
formulas.meaning: Reverse the inequality where $g(x) < 0$; check zeros of $g$ separately.

formulas.name: Profit condition
formulas.meaning: Maximum profit at the maximum of $P$.

formulas.name: Quadratic formula
formulas.meaning: Finds break-even points when $P$ is quadratic.

workedExamples.title: Three methods for one inequality
workedExamples.problem: Let $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = (x - 2)^2$. Find where $f(x) > g(x)$ and where $g(x) > f(x)$.
steps: **Quotient:** $\dfrac{x}{(x-2)^2} > 1$ on $(1, 4)$ except $x = 2$, where it is undefined; checking directly, $f(2) = 2 > g(2) = 0$.

workedExamples.title: Solve graphically: sin x > log x
steps: No algebraic method combines a trig and a log function, so graph both (radians).
$\sin x$ is above on $(0, 2.70)$ and $(7.33, 8.26)$; for $x > 10$, $\log x > 1$ so there are no more solutions.

workedExamples.title: Inventory control
workedExamples.problem: $C(n) = 1.5n + \dfrac{200\,000}{n}$, warehouse capacity 750. Find order sizes with $C(n) < 1500$ and the cheapest order size.
steps: Upward parabola → negative between the roots: $159 \le n \le 841$; with capacity, $159 \le n \le 750$.

workedExamples.title: Birdhouse profits
workedExamples.problem: Claire sells $n$ birdhouses a week at $(45 - n)$ dollars each. Costs: \$280 fixed plus \$8 per birdhouse. How many should she build to make a profit, and what is the best number?
workedExamples.answer: Build 11 to 26; 18 or 19 gives the maximum profit of \$62.

misconceptions.fact: Only where $g(x) > 0$. Where $g(x) < 0$ the inequality reverses, and where $g(x) = 0$ the quotient is undefined but $f$ and $g$ can still be compared.
Intersections found with technology are approximations – state them with appropriate rounding.
Profit is $R - C$. Its maximum generally occurs at a different quantity from the maximum of $R$.

misconceptions.myth: Solving $f(x) = g(x)$ is the whole answer to $f(x) > g(x)$.
misconceptions.fact: The equation only gives the boundary points; you must test the intervals between them.

realWorld.title: Housing developments
realWorld.body: Building too few houses doesn't cover fixed costs; building too many saturates the market. The profitable range lies between the break-even points of revenue and cost.

realWorld.title: Inventory
realWorld.body: Storage cost grows with order size, but frequent small orders cost more in shipping. The combined cost function has a 'sweet spot' and a range of acceptable order sizes.

realWorld.title: Town planning
realWorld.body: When a growing population $P(t)$ exceeds the number of people local services can supply, $N(t) - P(t) < 0$, the town needs new schools, clinics or transit.

realWorld.title: Movie theatre pricing
realWorld.body: Attendance falls as prices rise. Revenue and cost are combined functions of price, and the profitable price range comes from an inequality.

practice.question: Let $u(x) = x + 5$ and $v(x) = 2x$. Where is $u(x) > v(x)$?
For $u$, $v$ above, a student uses $\dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} > 1$ and gets $(0, 5)$. Explain the error.
practice.hint: What is the sign of $v(x)$ for $x < 0$?
practice.solution: For $x < 0$, $v(x) < 0$, so dividing reverses the inequality; also $v(0) = 0$. The quotient test only finds the part of the solution where $v > 0$. The full answer is $(-\infty, 5)$.

practice.question: Solve $\sin x < x$ for $x > 0$ (radians).
practice.hint: Compare the graphs near the origin.
practice.solution: $y = x$ is tangent to $\sin x$ at 0 and stays above it for $x > 0$, so the solution is all $x > 0$.

practice.question: A town's population is $P(t) = 2000(1.025)^t$ and services can supply $N(t) = 5000 + 57.5t$ people. When does demand exceed supply?
Revenue $R = -0.2n^2 + 3n$ and cost $C = 0.1n^2 + 0.4n + 2$ (thousands, $n$ thousand units). For what $n$ is there a profit?
practice.solution: $P = -0.3n^2 + 2.6n - 2 > 0$; roots $n = \dfrac{2.6 \pm \sqrt{4.36}}{0.6} \approx 0.85, 7.81$. Profit for about 0.85 to 7.81 thousand units.

summary: $f(x) > g(x)$ where the graph of $f$ is above the graph of $g$; intersections are the boundaries.
Three methods: compare graphs; difference $f - g > 0$; quotient $\dfrac fg > 1$ (only where $g > 0$, check zeros of $g$).
Inequalities like $\sin x > \log x$ are solved graphically or numerically with technology.
Profit occurs where $R > C$; break-even points bound the profitable region; maximum profit is the maximum of $R - C$.
Real problems often have a **range** of acceptable answers, given in interval notation and restricted by context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the points of intersection algebraically. Give the larger x-coordinate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the intervals where (i) $f(x) > g(x)$ and (ii) $g(x) > f(x)$.

parts.label: c

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $x = (x - {{a}})^2 \Rightarrow x^2 - {{2*a+1}}x + {{a*a}} = 0 \Rightarrow (x - {{r1}})(x - {{r2}}) = 0$.
Intersections $({{r1}}, {{r1}})$ and $({{r2}}, {{r2}})$.

**(b)** Test $x = {{a}}$ (between them): $f({{a}}) = {{a}} > g({{a}}) = 0$.
(i) $f(x) > g(x)$ on $({{r1}}, {{r2}})$.
(ii) $g(x) > f(x)$ on $(-\infty, {{r1}}) \cup ({{r2}}, \infty)$.

**(c)** $f(x) - g(x) = -x^2 + {{2*a+1}}x - {{a*a}} = -(x - {{r1}})(x - {{r2}})$, a downward parabola that is positive exactly on $({{r1}}, {{r2}})$ – confirming (b).

rubric.point: Sets f = g and factors correctly

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine and factor the difference function $y = f(x) - g(x)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve $f(x) > g(x)$ and $f(x) < g(x)$. Give the smaller boundary value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the points of intersection of the two graphs.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $f(x) - g(x) = x^2 - {{B}}x - {{m}}x + {{k+r1*r2}} - {{k}} = x^2 - {{r1+r2}}x + {{r1*r2}}$
$= (x - {{r1}})(x - {{r2}})$.

**(b)** Zeros $x = {{r1}}$ and $x = {{r2}}$. The difference is an upward parabola, so it is positive outside the zeros:
$f(x) > g(x)$ on $(-\infty, {{r1}}) \cup ({{r2}}, \infty)$ and $f(x) < g(x)$ on $({{r1}}, {{r2}})$.

**(c)** Intersection points: $({{r1}}, {{m*r1+k}})$ and $({{r2}}, {{m*r2+k}})$ (substitute into $g$).

rubric.point: Correct solution of f > g in interval notation

questions.text: There are three ways to illustrate where one function is greater than another: comparing the graphs, analysing the difference function, and analysing the quotient function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Summarize each method and give one advantage and one disadvantage of each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, with an example, why the quotient method can give a wrong answer.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)**
* **Visual:** graph both; read where one is above the other. + intuitive; − imprecise intersections, hard when curves are close.
* **Difference** $y = f - g$: solve $f - g > 0$. + one curve against the x-axis, works with algebra; − requires correct simplification.
* **Quotient** $y = f/g$ compared with 1. + shows relative size; − only valid where $g > 0$; undefined where $g = 0$.

**(b)** If $g(x) < 0$, multiplying both sides of $\frac{f}{g} > 1$ by $g$ reverses the inequality: $f < g$. Example: $f(x) = -1$, $g(x) = -2$: $f > g$, but $\frac{f}{g} = 0.5 < 1$. Where $g(x) = 0$ the quotient does not exist, but $f$ and $g$ can still be compared directly.

rubric.point: Gives a valid advantage and disadvantage for each
Explains why the quotient method fails for g < 0 or g = 0 with an example

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve $u(x) > v(x)$ using the difference function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student solves $\dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} > 1$ instead. What interval does the student get? Check a value of $x < 0$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the student's error.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $u(x) = v(x)$ at $x = {{c}}$. $u(x) - v(x) = {{c}} - x > 0$ for $x < {{c}}$. So $u > v$ on $(-\infty, {{c}})$.

**(b)** $\dfrac{u(x)}{v(x)} = \dfrac{x + {{c}}}{2x} > 1$. For $x > 0$ ($v > 0$): $x + {{c}} > 2x \Rightarrow x < {{c}}$, giving $(0, {{c}})$.
For $x < 0$ ($v < 0$): multiplying by $2x$ reverses: $x + {{c}} < 2x \Rightarrow x > {{c}}$ – impossible, so the quotient is **not** greater than 1 there. Yet $u > v$ for all $x < 0$ (e.g. $x = -1$: $u = {{c-1}} > v = -2$).

**(c)** The quotient test misses $(-\infty, 0]$ because $v(x) \le 0$ there: dividing by a negative reverses the inequality, and $v(0) = 0$ makes the quotient undefined. The correct solution is $(-\infty, {{c}})$.

rubric.point: Correct analysis of the quotient on x > 0
Shows the quotient test fails for x < 0 with a check
States the correct full solution and explains the error

questions.text: A store's cost of shipping and storing $n$ units is $C(n) = {{a}}n + \dfrac{ {{b}} }{n}$ dollars. The warehouse holds at most {{cap}} units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the shape of the graph of $C(n)$ and state the domain of interest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the range of order sizes that keeps costs below \${{L}}. Give the smallest order size.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use technology or reasoning to estimate the order size with the lowest cost.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why might the cheapest order size not be the best number to order?

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $C$ is the superposition of a linear function ${{a}}n$ (storage grows with order size) and a rational function $\frac{ {{b}} }{n}$ (shipping cost per order spread over fewer units). Domain of interest: $0 < n \le {{cap}}$.

**(b)** $C(n) < {{L}}$: multiply by $n > 0$: ${{a}}n^2 - {{L}}n + {{b}} < 0$.
$n = \dfrac{ {{L}} \pm \sqrt{ {{L}}^2 - 4({{a}})({{b}}) } }{ 2({{a}}) } \approx {{(L-sqrt(L*L-4*a*b))/(2*a):4}}$ or ${{(L+sqrt(L*L-4*a*b))/(2*a):4}}$.
The parabola opens up, so the inequality holds between the roots: about {{ceil((L-sqrt(L*L-4*a*b))/(2*a))}} to {{floor((L+sqrt(L*L-4*a*b))/(2*a))}} units, and no more than {{cap}} because of the warehouse.

**(c)** Optimum (minimum cost) from the graph: $n = \sqrt{ {{b}}/{{a}} } \approx {{sqrt(b/a):3}}$ units, cost $\approx \text{\textdollar}{{2*sqrt(a*b):4}}$.

**(d)** The cheapest order may not match demand: too few units means lost sales; too many ties up money and space.

rubric.point: Explains the shape as linear + rational with domain
Rearranges to a quadratic inequality correctly (n > 0)
Correct roots via the quadratic formula
Correct whole-number range, applying the capacity
Correct optimum order size and cost
Explains why the optimum may not be best

questions.text: Claire builds and sells $n$ birdhouses a week for $({{P0}} - n)$ dollars each. Her weekly costs are \${{F}} fixed plus \${{v}} per birdhouse. She sells every birdhouse she makes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for her total weekly cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation for her weekly revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an inequality for the conditions under which Claire makes a profit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: How many birdhouses should she build each week to make a profit?

parts.label: e
parts.text: What is the optimum number to build, and what is the maximum weekly profit?

rubric.point: Solves the quadratic inequality and gives whole-number range
Correct optimum number and maximum profit

questions.text: A developer can build up to 500 houses. Revenue is $R(n) = {{a}}\sqrt{n}$ million dollars and cost is $C(n) = {{F}} + {{v}}n$ million dollars, where $n$ is the number of houses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the break-even points. Give the larger number of houses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What are the minimum and maximum numbers of houses she should build?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many houses give the maximum profit, and what is that profit?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the developer could increase her profits. Support your answer with mathematical reasoning.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** Break-even: ${{a}}\sqrt{n} = {{F}} + {{v}}n$. Let $u = \sqrt{n}$: ${{v}}u^2 - {{a}}u + {{F}} = 0$.
$u = \dfrac{ {{a}} \pm \sqrt{ {{a*a}} - 4({{v}})({{F}}) } }{ 2({{v}}) } \approx {{(a-sqrt(a*a-4*v*F))/(2*v):4}}$ or ${{(a+sqrt(a*a-4*v*F))/(2*v):4}}$.
$n = u^2 \approx {{((a-sqrt(a*a-4*v*F))/(2*v))^2:3}}$ or ${{((a+sqrt(a*a-4*v*F))/(2*v))^2:3}}$ houses.

**(b)** $R > C$ between the break-even points: build from about {{ceil(((a-sqrt(a*a-4*v*F))/(2*v))^2)}} to {{floor(((a+sqrt(a*a-4*v*F))/(2*v))^2)}} houses.

**(c)** $P = {{a}}u - {{F}} - {{v}}u^2$ is a downward parabola in $u$ with vertex $u = \dfrac{ {{a}} }{ 2({{v}}) }$, so $n = \left(\dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{2*v}} }\right)^2 \approx {{(a/(2*v))^2:3}}$ houses, $P_{max} = \dfrac{ {{a*a}} }{ 4({{v}}) } - {{F}} \approx {{a*a/(4*v)-F:3}}$ million.

**(d)** To increase profits she could reduce fixed or variable costs (lowering the cost line) or increase prices (raising the revenue curve), which widens the profitable range.

rubric.point: Sets up the break-even equation and substitutes u = √n
Correct optimum number of houses and maximum profit
Sensible suggestions linked to the graph

questions.text: The number of people who attend a movie showing is $N(p) = -(p + 7)(p - {{q}})$, where $p$ is the ticket price in dollars (minimum price \$5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For what prices is $N(p) > 0$? What does this suggest about the maximum ticket price?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many people attend at \${{p1}}?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the revenue function $R(p) = pN(p)$, state where $R(p) > 0$, and find $R({{p1}})$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Do the maxima of $N(p)$ and $R(p)$ occur at the same price? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $N(p) > 0$ when $-7 < p < {{q}}$. With the minimum price, attendance is positive for $5 \le p < {{q}}$, so \${{q}} is the maximum realistic price.

**(b)** $N({{p1}}) = -({{p1+7}})({{p1-q}}) = {{-(p1+7)*(p1-q)}}$ people.

**(c)** Revenue $R(p) = pN(p) = -p(p + 7)(p - {{q}})$, a cubic. $R > 0$ on the same interval $5 \le p < {{q}}$ (since $p > 0$). $R({{p1}}) = \text{\textdollar}{{-p1*(p1+7)*(p1-q)}}$.

**(d)** The maxima of $N$ and $R$ occur at different prices: $N$ is largest at $p = \frac{ {{q}} - 7}{2}$, which is below the \$5 minimum, while $R$ also depends on the price itself, so its maximum (found by graphing) is at a higher price.

rubric.point: Correct interval for N > 0 and maximum realistic price
Correct attendance at the given price
Explains why the maxima of N and R differ

questions.text: A toy company's projected revenue for a new product is $R = -0.2n^2 + 3n$ and its cost is $C = 0.1n^2 + 0.4n + {{c0}}$, where $n$ is thousands of units and $R$, $C$ are in thousands of dollars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the points of intersection of $R$ and $C$ and explain their significance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the region where $R > C$. Why is it important?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use $P = R - C$ to find the optimum number of units and the maximum profit.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest reasons why the revenue and cost curves are not linear.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** Set $R = C$: $-0.3n^2 + 2.6n - {{c0}} = 0$, i.e. $0.3n^2 - 2.6n + {{c0}} = 0$.
$n = \dfrac{2.6 \pm \sqrt{6.76 - {{1.2*c0:3}} }}{0.6} \approx {{(2.6-sqrt(6.76-1.2*c0))/0.6:3}}$ or ${{(2.6+sqrt(6.76-1.2*c0))/0.6:3}}$. Two intersection points – the break-even quantities.

**(b)** $R > C$ between them: about {{(2.6-sqrt(6.76-1.2*c0))/0.6:3}} to {{(2.6+sqrt(6.76-1.2*c0))/0.6:3}} thousand units. This is the profitable region.

**(c)** $P = R - C = -0.3n^2 + 2.6n - {{c0}}$. Vertex $n = \dfrac{2.6}{0.6} \approx 4.33$ thousand units.
$P_{max} = -0.3(4.333)^2 + 2.6(4.333) - {{c0}} \approx {{2.6*2.6/1.2-c0:3}}$ thousand dollars, about ${{(2.6*2.6/1.2-c0)/4.333:3}}$ thousand dollars per thousand units (≈ \${{(2.6*2.6/1.2-c0)/4.333:3}} per unit).

**(d)** Revenue is concave down because the price must drop to sell more units; cost is concave up because producing very large amounts needs overtime, more equipment and storage.

rubric.point: Correct break-even equation and both solutions
Correct profit function and optimum quantity
Reasonable explanation of the curve shapes

questions.text: A town's projected population is $P(t) = 2000(1.025)^t$, $t$ years from now. Local services can supply $N(t) = 5000 + 57.5t$ people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine $y = N(t) - P(t)$ and explain what it represents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend of this function.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When is $N(t) - P(t) < 0$? Explain what this means.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what $y = \dfrac{N(t)}{P(t)}$ represents.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $y = N(t) - P(t) = 5000 + 57.5t - 2000(1.025)^t$. It is the surplus capacity of services (positive) or the shortfall (negative). At $t = 0$ it is 3000.

**(b)** It increases at first (the linear part grows faster initially), then the exponential term takes over and it decreases, crossing zero.

**(c)** Using technology, $N(t) - P(t) = 0$ at $t \approx 57.7$. So $N(t) - P(t) < 0$ for $t > 57.7$: after about 58 years the population exceeds what services can supply.

**(d)** $\dfrac{N(t)}{P(t)}$ is services available per person; it starts at 2.5 and decreases, falling below 1 at $t \approx 57.7$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find all points of intersection of $y = x^2$ and $y = 2^x$. Give the negative one to three decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the inequality. Show how you tested the intervals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there are no solutions for $x > 4$.

questions.modelAnswer:
This mixes a polynomial and an exponential, so solve graphically.

**(a)** Intersections: $x = 2$ ($4 = 4$), $x = 4$ ($16 = 16$), and one negative value found with technology, $x \approx -0.767$.

**(b)** Test each interval:
* $x = -2$: $4 > 0.25$ ✓
* $x = 0$: $0 > 1$ ✗
* $x = 3$: $9 > 8$ ✓
* $x = 5$: $25 > 32$ ✗

So $x^2 > 2^x$ on $(-\infty, -0.767) \cup (2, 4)$.

**(c)** For $x > 4$, the exponential's rate of change grows in proportion to its value, so $2^x$ outgrows $x^2$ forever.

rubric.point: Explains end behaviour for large x

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the regions where (i) $f(x) > g(x)$ (ii) $g(x) > f(x)$. Give the boundary to two decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two different ways to illustrate this inequality graphically.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a real-world scenario that these functions could model.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** Using technology, the graphs intersect at $x \approx 9.31$ ($y \approx 5.46$).
(i) $f(x) > g(x)$ for $x > 9.31$. (ii) $g(x) > f(x)$ for $x < 9.31$.

**(b)** Two ways: (1) graph both and shade between where $f$ is above $g$; (2) graph $y = f(x) - g(x)$ and show it is positive for $x > 9.31$.

**(c)** Scenario: $f$ is the value (thousands) of an investment growing 20%/year; $g$ is a depreciating asset (car, losing 8% a year) plus \$5000 savings. The investment overtakes after about 9.3 years.

rubric.point: Correct regions for f > g and g > f

questions.text: Solve $\sin x > \log x$ (radians) and explain your method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why can't this be solved algebraically?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the inequality. Give the first intersection to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why there are no solutions for large $x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** A trig function and a logarithm cannot be combined algebraically, so use technology: graph $y = \sin x$ and $y = \log x$.

**(b)** Intersections: $x \approx 2.70$, $7.33$, $8.26$. Since $\log x$ needs $x > 0$:
$\sin x > \log x$ on $(0, 2.70) \cup (7.33, 8.26)$.

**(c)** For $x \ge 10$, $\log x \ge 1 \ge \sin x$ (with equality impossible at the same time beyond 10, since $\log$ keeps increasing), so there are no further solutions.

rubric.point: Explains why there are no solutions beyond x = 10

questions.text: Write functions that satisfy each condition and justify each one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: $f(x) > g(x)$ on $(-\infty, \infty)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: $f(x) > g(x)$ on regular periodic intervals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: $f(x) > g(x)$ only on $(0, 4)$. Give two different solutions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: $f(x) < g(x)$ on $(-1, 1)$ and $f(x) > g(x)$ on $(-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty)$.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $f(x) = x^2 + 1$, $g(x) = 0$: $f > g$ for all real $x$ since $x^2 + 1 \ge 1$.

**(b)** $f(x) = \sin x$, $g(x) = 0$: $f > g$ on $(2n\pi, (2n+1)\pi)$ – regular periodic intervals.

**(c)** Need $f - g$ positive exactly on $(0, 4)$: $f(x) - g(x) = -x(x - 4)$. Choose $g(x) = x$, $f(x) = -x^2 + 5x$. Another solution: $f(x) = 4$, $g(x) = (x - 2)^2$.

**(d)** For $f(x) < g(x)$ on $(-1, 1)$ and $f > g$ outside: $f(x) = x^2$, $g(x) = 1$, since $x^2 - 1 < 0 \iff -1 < x < 1$.

rubric.point: Valid example for all real x
Valid example for (0, 4) using a difference with zeros 0 and 4

questions.text: A business has cost $C(n) = {{F}} + {{v}}n$ and revenue $R(n) = {{p}}n$, where $n$ is the number of units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the break-even point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the regions where (i) $C > R$ (ii) $R > C$, and interpret each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe $y = R - C$, and explain how its graph changes if the slope of the cost function increases or decreases.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $R = C$: ${{p}}n = {{F}} + {{v}}n \Rightarrow n = \dfrac{ {{F}} }{ {{p-v}} } \approx {{F/(p-v):3}}$.

**(b)** (i) $C > R$ for $0 \le n < {{F/(p-v):3}}$ – a loss. (ii) $R > C$ for $n > {{F/(p-v):3}}$ – a profit.

**(c)** $y = R - C = {{p-v}}n - {{F}}$: below the n-axis for losses, above it for profit. Increasing the slope of the cost function (higher variable cost) moves the break-even point right and lowers potential profit; decreasing it does the opposite.

rubric.point: Correct regions for C > R and R > C with interpretation
Explains effect of changing the cost slope

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine and factor $y = f(x) - g(x)$. Give its positive zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve $f(x) > g(x)$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve $f(x) \le g(x)$.

questions.modelAnswer:
**(a)** $f(x) - g(x) = x^3 - {{p+q}}x = x(x^2 - {{p+q}}) = x(x - \sqrt{ {{p+q}} })(x + \sqrt{ {{p+q}} })$.
Zeros: $0, \pm\sqrt{ {{p+q}} } \approx \pm{{sqrt(p+q):3}}$.

**(b)** Sign chart (cubic, positive leading coefficient): − on $(-\infty, -{{sqrt(p+q):3}})$, + on $(-{{sqrt(p+q):3}}, 0)$, − on $(0, {{sqrt(p+q):3}})$, + on $({{sqrt(p+q):3}}, \infty)$.
$f(x) > g(x)$ on $(-\sqrt{ {{p+q}} }, 0) \cup (\sqrt{ {{p+q}} }, \infty)$.

**(c)** $f(x) \le g(x)$ on $(-\infty, -\sqrt{ {{p+q}} }] \cup [0, \sqrt{ {{p+q}} }]$.

rubric.point: Correct sign analysis and solution of f > g
Correct solution of f ≤ g with endpoints included
